title: What are some movies that people have picked to death with analysis?

commenti.body:
>Symbolism in every single frame beyond what a filmmaker would strive for, wild parallels, the hysterical (in the crazy way) predictions of the Chernobyl Disaster. It all reminded me of my film teacher making dramatic gestures of reading film, which he did to prove a point and not to actually read the film. We did this with so many movies but the intention was to imagine and hone the craft of understanding cinema.

In general, the picking apart of films - especially Kubrick films, The Shining included - as pots-pourris of literal-minded symbols, is pseudo-intellectual and profoundly anti-poetic. Neither the meaning nor the brilliance of the Shining is hidden in the patterns on the carpeting in the Overlook hotel: the way to experience the film is through its aesthetics, not through objects tucked into the corners of the frame: its a work of art, not a puzzle.

Rerumdex in three, two, one...

I don't know, I would argue that those "objects tucked into the corners of the frame" are part of its aesthetics and if there are elements that pique someone's interest in the midst of analysis they're worth looking at. 

*Especially* when the film isn't overt in its themes, because in those cases the viewer is actually asked to look closer and "inspect" in hopes of finding clues. 

I do agree that it can lead to a pseudo-intellectual way of looking at film, but that's only when one takes it too far.

>Especially when the film isn't overt in its themes, because in those cases the viewer is actually asked to look closer and "inspect" in hopes of finding clues.

I would suggest is asked to peer closer to the narrative, the characters, the overall aesthetic. Once you start looking for physical "clues" in the frame, in the way those infernal Kubrickians do, it loses its point, and one starts missing the forest for the trees.
If you're *only* looking for physical clues, sure, but you can't just ignore them entirely.
I almost clapped as I read this. What have you done to me?

What I mean by physical clues is stuff like "Oh look! The pattern on the carpets in the Overlook is symbolic of this and that!" or "look, the aspect ratio of the panels behind Floyd in the conference room in 2001 is like this Renaissance painting, which proves X" or "at the premiere of 2001, there was a projection glitch at THIS moment in the film, surely that was intentional and symbolic of this or that."

THAT kind of reading into symbolism.

One thing I’ve always thought about the hyper analysis of films is that it can’t all possibly be true.  There are some truly incredible, profound, thoughtful, and genuinely deep directors out there.  That much is true.  But I simultaneously find it very hard to believe that every little thing people analyze in a particular film was actually intentional.  Take Lynch, Kubrick, or any other hyper analyzed director for instance.  They’re work is undoubtedly complex and filled with motifs, metaphors, and more.  But there is no way that every little thing film lovers pick apart was actually inentional.

I find it hard to believe that every number, carpet, door, toy, piece of paper, word, phrase, etc. from The Shining has a specific meaning or symbolism that Kubrick specially prescribed to them.

And every weird, dreamlike sequence that Lynch puts together doesn’t always have a meaning.  Sometimes I doubt Lynch even knows what they mean.  He’s talked at length about how he’s inspired by feelings, dreams, and emotions instead of concrete ideas and plot lines.  I feel like a lot of the things people over analyze in his films are actually meant to evoke a dreamlike, rich-in-feeling, experience rather than an actual commentary or deeper meaning.

And this holds true for every director that ever lived.  There are many things they do intentionally, but sometimes I feel like people assign meaning to things that never really had it.  And part of the fun and art of film is people being able to put there own interpretations into a film, so most directors don’t dispute many of peoples analyzations.

I don't really have any problem with any of that if it's placed into the context of a larger, more comprehensive reading of the film as a whole. One little comment like those you mention isn't much on itself, but if it fits within a larger argument (and other evidence), what's the problem? 

Of course I hate language like "proves", or "surely". Instead, I suggest using wording that is less overt, like "suggests" or "could represent". 

I guess what I'd generally say is that I tend to err on the side of *more* analysis, not less. "Overanalyzing" is better than no analysis at all (which is increasingly the case as the "it's just a movie" people gain more tread in the film world).

I always laugh when people pick The Shining apart it is a fantastic Horror/Thriller but  they never talk about the film that scared Kubrick more than any other in The Vanishing which I found a lot more intriguing. I wouldn’t consider the Shining top 5 in horror personally but the people that love the film are psychotic like the Scorsese Goodfellas crowd.

I will add that a film is ultimately made by a creative team. Many details are certainly not the director’s request, and this is rarely acknowledged because it challenges the aura of mystery and glorification directors are usually surrounded by.

Any movie in the top 250 of IMDB or on those lists of Rotten Tomatoes. It really pisses me off when I wanna read peoples views and reviews on High and Low and all I can find are videos of blocking and framing which is sick but I wanna learn more about Japan during that time. I watch the Asphalt Jungle and I can barely find any discussions on the film but if I want an analysis of Heat there’s 400,000 conversations about that it’s mind boggling.

Absolutely.  Not everything is done by the director.  If the director is also the writer, than yeah, it adds a little more weight to that mystique, but a film is ultimately a collaborative piece of art.

Even with writer/directors, the photography, production design, sound and editing are led by artists just as talented as the director. Great directors know about these departments’ influence and importance, so they collaborate with equally great creatives.

Honestly, don't worry about "intention", it only hampers film analysis. So much of what goes into a film likely happens on an unconscious level, so what's the point of focusing on what the director "intended"?

Let the film speak for itself.

>I wouldn’t consider the Shining top 5 in horror personally

Well, if we judge it as a horror film and strictly as a horror film, it does have one major shortcoming...its not scary. Not in any usual sense of the word, at least.
